主要内容: Fidel Castro's biggest financial regrets reveal his acknowledgment of past decisions that impacted Cuba's economic stability. During a meeting with Bill Rhodes, a former Citigroup executive, Castro admitted regret over expelling the International Monetary Fund (IMF) from Cuba during the early days of the communist revolution. He believed that staying a member of the IMF, along with the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, could have provided crucial support for Cuba's economic challenges. Additionally, Castro expressed regret over placing Ernesto 'Che' Guevara in charge of the Cuban central bank, acknowledging that Guevara lacked financial expertise. Guevara, known for his role in the Cuban Revolution and his brutal tactics against political enemies, later led the seizure of American banks in Cuba, including branches of Citigroup, Bank of America, and JPMorgan Chase. These actions contributed to Cuba's debt issues, with an estimated $5 billion still outstanding from the mid-1980s. Fidel Castro has expressed significant financial regrets, particularly regarding the nationalization of Cuban assets and the impact of the U.S. trade embargo. In a conversation with former U.S. Ambassador to Cuba, Peter Rhodes, Castro stated that he did not believe Cuba owed Citigroup any money for the seized banks, as Citigroup had frozen Cuban assets held in New York. This sentiment was further elaborated in an essay published in a Communist Party newspaper following the reopening of the U.S. embassy in Cuba after 54 years. Castro argued that the United States owes Cuba "many millions of dollars" in damages from the trade embargo, which lasted for half a century. He also criticized the U.S. for removing the dollar from the gold standard in 1971. Rhodes, who had previously disagreed with Castro's stance on debts to Citigroup, noted that the government of Cuba owed them on loans that could not be collected due to nationalization. Reflecting on the conversation, Rhodes called it "a fascinating conversation."
